To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cross‐section of nerve bundles was the significant factor in the success of limb regeneration in the amputated wingbuds of chick embryos.

nerve regeneration in the chick limb is dependent on the presence of a critical mass of axoplasm in the amputation (stump) wound, but that nerve regeneration does not depend on the number of nerve bundles.
nerve bundles in limbs that regenerate contain significantly greater cross‐sectional areas than in limbs that do not regenerate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the peripheral nerve in limb regeneration in the chicken embryo.
the factors which control the regeneration and differentiation of the limb.
the problem of how a nerve can induce a limb to regenerate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amount of nerve axoplasm at the amputation site is the essential requirement for successful regeneration.
the threshold quantity of nerve needed for regeneration is 0.2 mm2.
the threshold for regeneration in the chick limb bud is 1.5 × 10 ^{4} µm ^{2} of nerve axoplasm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the threshold quantity of nerve for regeneration is 0.1 mm ^{2} of cross‐sectional nerve area.
the threshold quantity of axoplasm is about 2–3 times the cross‐section of one nerve bundle.

the amount of nerve axoplasm available is the critical factor in determining the ability of an amputated appendage to regenerate, and that the number of nerve bundles and/or their cross‐sectional areas are the best quantitative measures of this axoplasm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of nerve required for regeneration is not the number of nerve bundles, but rather the total area of nerve cross section.
the amount of nerve axoplasm available is more important than the number of nerve bundles.
the amount of nerve required for regeneration is a function of the number of axon bundles and their cross‐sectional areas.
